Package tracking

You run the tracking page for a parcel company. People refresh it again and again while they wait for a delivery, and depots send a scan every time a parcel moves. Keep the page fast, lose at most the last minute of scans in a failure (scanners keep a copy and can resend), and make sure a broken text-message service cannot slow anything down. The brief

You run the tracking page for a parcel company. People refresh it again and again while they wait for a delivery, and depots send a scan every time a parcel moves. Keep the page fast, lose at most the last minute of scans in a failure (scanners keep a copy and can resend), and make sure a broken text-message service cannot slow anything down.

Think of parcel tracking like UPS.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
20 million people a month (approx.)
Audience in plain numbers
20,000,000 people per month
Normal peak
≈ 3,000 requests per second
Request mix
Read: 90%; Write: 7%; Notification: 3%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Read: ≈ 800 ms; Write: ≈ 1,100 ms
Successful requests
99.9%
Data safety
At most 1 minute of writes may be lost.
Monthly budget
≈ $16,000
Data at rest
≈ 5 TB
Where users are
North America: 100%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Read: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds; Notification: 900 seconds
Minimum retained history
90 days on authoritative stores
Personal reads
20% of reads are private; a shared public copy cannot answer them.

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • About 15 million parcels a day, 8 scans each, about 0.5 KB per scan: roughly 60 GB a day, 90 days kept hot (approx.).
  • Reads are tracking-page lookups, writes are depot scans, notifications are text and push alerts.
  • The peak is a holiday-season evening. All numbers are rough approximations.
  • Scored data retention: at least 90 days on active authoritative stores. Copies used only for search or reports can be rebuilt. Local device history and rollup policies still require the separate protocol check.
  • Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

Questions that shape the design

Do tracking answers have to be up to the second?

No. A status that is up to a minute old is fine. People care that the page opens fast and the next step is right.

Can a depot scan be lost or counted twice?

At most the last minute of scans, and only in a failure: scanners keep a copy and resend when the network drops, so the same scan can arrive twice. Counting it twice would show the wrong history.

What happens when the text-message service is down?

Alerts can arrive later. The tracking page must keep working and no alert may be dropped.

The traffic day

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 10:15 · Dependency outage

    An outside service fails calls during an outage.

    Failed calls: 100%. The failure lasts ≈ 1,200 seconds.

  2. 18:30 · Viral spike

    A post blows up. Traffic climbs to several times normal within minutes.

    Traffic reaches 4 times the scheduled load; rises over 600 seconds, holds for 3,600 seconds and eases over 3,600 seconds.

What a strong design has to handle

  • Most of the load is people checking the same parcel again and again. What could remember an answer for a minute?
  • A 60 second cache means a status can be a minute old. For parcels that is fine; for a stock price it would not be.
  • Collapsing misses protects the database when the cache is cold, at the price of a few people waiting for one shared refill.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.

Concepts to practise

  • Remembering answers
  • Waiting instead of breaking

Related problems

  • Easy

    Lab results portal

    Labs send results to a portal, patients get a notice that a result is ready and open it. When the notice goes to thousands of people at the same minute, they all open the portal at once. Nobody should get the same notice twice.

  • Medium

    Fleet telemetry

    A freight company has 150,000 trucks that each send a batch of sensor readings every 30 seconds. Dispatchers watch live maps and analysts run reports. You must take in every batch, keep a month of detail cheaply, and survive the moments when thousands of trucks come back online at once.

  • Hard

    Maps and routing

    You run a maps app with places, routes and live traffic. Map pictures never change much, but route lookups, place search and traffic from moving phones do. Soon a whole new continent will start using it. Keep maps fast everywhere without paying to serve the same picture twice.

  • Easy

    URL shortener

    People paste a long web address and get back a short one. Millions of other people then tap that short link, so reading is almost everything. Keep every tap fast, and never lose a link.
